--- title: "Hands-on Exercise 8" author: "Kock Si Min" date: October 19, 2024 date-modified: "last-modified" toc: true execute: eval: true echo: true freeze: true warning: false message: false --- # Geographically Weighted Predictive Models ## 8.1 Overview Predictive modelling uses statistical learning or machine learning techniques to predict outcomes. By and large, the event one wants to predict is in the future. However, a set of known outcome and predictors (also known as variables) will be used to calibrate the predictive models. Geospatial predictive modelling is conceptually rooted in the principle that the occurrences of events being modeled are limited in distribution. **When geographically referenced data are used, occurrences of events are neither uniform nor random in distribution over space.** There are geospatial factors (infrastructure, sociocultural, topographic, etc.) that constrain and influence where the locations of events occur. **Geospatial predictive modeling attempts to describe those constraints and influences by spatially correlating occurrences of historical geospatial locations with environmental factors that represent those constraints and influences.** ### 8.1.1 Learning outcomes In this exercise, we will build a predictive model by using geographical random forest method. The hands-on exercise includes: - preparing train and test data sets by using appropriate data sampling methods, - calibrating predictive models by using both geospatial statistical learning and machine learning methods, - comparing and selecting the best model for predicting the future outcome, - predicting the future outcomes by using the best model calibrated. ## 8.2 The Data - **Aspatial dataset**: - [HDB Resale data](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_8b84c4ee58e3cfc0ece0d773c8ca6abc/view): a list of HDB resale transacted prices in Singapore from Jan 2017 onwards. It is in csv format which can be downloaded from Data.gov.sg. - **Geospatial dataset**: - [*MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL*](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_d14da225fccf921049ab64238ff473d9/view): a polygon feature data providing information of URA 2014 Master Plan Planning Subzone boundary data. It is in ESRI shapefile format. This data set was also downloaded from Data.gov.sg - **Locational factors with geographic coordinates**: - Downloaded from **Data.gov.sg**. - [**Eldercare**](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_3545b068e3f3506c56b2cb6b6117b884/view) data is a list of eldercare in Singapore. It is in shapefile format. - [**Hawker Centre**](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_4a086da0a5553be1d89383cd90d07ecd/view) data is a list of hawker centres in Singapore. It is in geojson format. - [**Parks**](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_0542d48f0991541706b58059381a6eca/view) data is a list of parks in Singapore. It is in geojson format. - [**Supermarket**](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_cac2c32f01960a3ad7202a99c27268a0/view) data is a list of supermarkets in Singapore. It is in geojson format. - [**CHAS clinics**](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_548c33ea2d99e29ec63a7cc9edcccedc/view) data is a list of CHAS clinics in Singapore. It is in geojson format. - [**Childcare service**](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_5d668e3f544335f8028f546827b773b4/view) data is a list of childcare services in Singapore. It is in geojson format. - [**Kindergartens**](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_7fe9a72b1afff18e48111772c8d0fd39/view) data is a list of kindergartens in Singapore. It is in geojson format. - Downloaded from **Datamall.lta.gov.sg**. - [**MRT**](https://datamall.lta.gov.sg/content/datamall/en/search_datasets.html?searchText=train) data is a list of MRT/LRT stations in Singapore with the station names and codes. It is in shapefile format. - [**Bus stops**](https://datamall.lta.gov.sg/content/datamall/en/search_datasets.html?searchText=train) data is a list of bus stops in Singapore. It is in shapefile format. - **Locational factors without geographic coordinates**: - Downloaded from **Data.gov.sg**. - **Primary school** data is extracted from the list on [General information of schools](https://data.gov.sg/datasets/d_688b934f82c1059ed0a6993d2a829089/view) from data.gov portal. It is in csv format. - Retrieved/Scraped from **other sources** - **CBD** coordinates obtained from Google. - **Shopping malls** data is a list of Shopping malls in Singapore obtained from [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_shopping_malls_in_Singapore). - **Good primary schools** is a list of primary schools that are ordered in ranking in terms of popularity and this can be found at [Local Salary Forum](https://www.salary.sg/2021/best-primary-schools-2021-by-popularity). ## 8.3 Installing and Loading R packages The code chunk below performs 3 tasks: - A list called packages will be created and will consists of all the R packages required to accomplish this exercise. - Check if R packages on package have been installed in R and if not, they will be installed. - After all the R packages have been installed, they will be loaded. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load(sf,spdep,GWmodel,SpatialML,tmap,rsample,Metrics, tidyverse,spatstat,kableExtra) ``` ::: ## 8.4 Preparing Data ### 8.4.1 Reading data file to rds For the hands-on exercise, Prof Kam provided a "mdata.rds" file which comprises the data stated in Section [8.2 The Data] above. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mdata <- read_rds("data/rds/mdata.rds") mdata ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Simple feature collection with 15901 features and 17 fields Geometry type: POINT Dimension: XY Bounding box: xmin: 11597.31 ymin: 28217.39 xmax: 42623.63 ymax: 48741.06 Projected CRS: SVY21 / Singapore TM # A tibble: 15,901 × 18 resale_price floor_area_sqm storey_order remaining_lease_mths PROX_CBD 1 330000 92 1 684 8.82 2 360000 91 3 738 9.84 3 370000 92 1 733 9.56 4 375000 99 2 700 9.61 5 380000 92 2 715 8.35 6 380000 92 4 732 9.49 7 385000 92 3 706 8.96 8 395000 92 2 745 9.81 9 395000 93 4 731 10.3 10 395000 91 3 725 10.4 # ℹ 15,891 more rows # ℹ 13 more variables: PROX_ELDERLYCARE , PROX_HAWKER , # PROX_MRT , PROX_PARK , PROX_GOOD_PRISCH , PROX_MALL , # PROX_CHAS , PROX_SUPERMARKET , WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN , # WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE , WITHIN_350M_BUS , # WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH , geometry ``` ::: ::: We note that the object is a simple feature data frame, with point geometry and 15901 features and 17 fields. The projected coordinates system is SVY21. ::: callout-note ## In-class note from Prof Kam - note that proximity to xx are derived values - note that there are some inconsistencies in the values i.e. some too small - **to overcome overlap, need to use st_jitter():** - prof shared that there is either amount or factor - **is better to use amount since its based on units of coordinates** - put amount as 2 - don't use v big figures **but also don't use decimal points as when there's rounding, it might round to 0 then back to square one** - must be careful about the distance set to avoid jittering the point out of the boundary ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mdata <- mdata %>% st_jitter(amount = 2) ``` ::: ::: ### 8.4.2 Data Sampling We split the data set into training (65%) and test (35%) data sets by using *initial_split()* of [**rsample**](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/) package. rsample is a [**tidymodels**](https://www.tidymodels.org/) package (collection of tools to do modelling, new framework to build modelling pipeline): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1234) resale_split <- initial_split(mdata, prop = 6.5/10,) train_data <- training(resale_split) test_data <- testing(resale_split) ``` ::: ::: callout-note ## In-class note from Prof Kam - note that the above is random sampling method - 65% is train and 35% is test - can immediately pull out training and test data set as separate datasets - always save the training and test datasets as new rds files ::: We save the train and test data sets as new rds files and load them into the R environment to avoid rerunning the above step: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_rds(train_data,"data/rds/train_data.rds") write_rds(test_data,"data/rds/test_data.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train_data <- read_rds("data/rds/train_data.rds") test_data <- read_rds("data/rds/test_data.rds") ``` ::: ## 8.5 Computing Correlation Matrix Before loading the predictors into a predictive model, it is always good practice to use the correlation matrix to examine for signs of multicollinearity: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mdata_nogeo <- mdata %>% st_drop_geometry() corrplot::corrplot(cor(mdata_nogeo[,2:17]), diag = FALSE, order = "AOE", tl.pos = "td", tl.cex = 0.5, number.cex = 0.7, method = "number", type = "upper") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: callout-note ## In-class note from Prof Kam: - another way to generate the correlation matrix is using the code chunk below: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggstatsplot::ggcorrmat(mdata_nogeo[,2:17]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: Note that matrix reorder is very important for mining the hidden structure and pattern in the matrix. There are four methods in corrplot (parameter order), namely “AOE”, “FPC”, “hclust”, “alphabet”. In the code chunk above, “AOE” order is used. It orders the variables by using the *angular order of the eigenvectors* method suggested by [Michael Friendly](https://www.datavis.ca/papers/corrgram.pdf). The correlation matrix above shows that **all correlation values are below 0.8, there is hence no sign of multicollinearity.** ## 8.6 Building a non-spatial multiple linear regression We build a multiple linear regression model using the code chunk below: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} price_mlr <- lm(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK+ PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, data = train_data) ``` ::: ::: callout-note ## In-class note from Prof Kam - note that only use training data to calibrate the model, will not use test data to calibrate - we can use olsrr to generate report - provide a more organised way to look through results: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} olsrr::ols_regress(price_mlr) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Summary -------------------------------------------------------------------------- R 0.859 RMSE 61604.120 R-Squared 0.737 MSE 3800583670.022 Adj. The code chunk below is used to determine the adaptive bandwidth with CV method used to determine the optimal bandwidth: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bw_adaptive <- bw.gwr(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK+ PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, data = train_data_sp, approach = "CV", kernel = "gaussian", adaptive = TRUE, longlat = FALSE) ``` ::: ::: callout-note ## In-class note from Prof Kam - Note that gw can now handle non-sp data format hence the codes below use train_data and test_data directly and not the sp formats - Predictive Modelling with MLR: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} We also use the adaptive bandwidth with CV method: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gwr_bw_test_adaptive <- bw.gwr(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK+ PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, data = test_data_sp, approach = "CV", kernel = "gaussian", adaptive = TRUE, longlat = FALSE) ``` ::: The result shows that 25 neighbour points will be the optimal bandwidth to be used if adaptive bandwidth is used for the test data set. ![](images/clipboard-4229058609.png) We save the results as a new rds file to avoid re-running the above step which can take a while: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_rds(gwr_bw_test_adaptive,"data/rds/gwr_bw_test_adaptive.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gwr_bw_test_adaptive <- read_rds("data/rds/gwr_bw_test_adaptive.rds") gwr_bw_test_adaptive ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 25 ``` ::: ::: ### 8.7.7 Computing predicted values of the test data We then compute the predicted HDB resale prices from the test data set. It is noted that if we were to use bw = 25 from gwr_bw_test_adaptive above, we would get an error "Error: inv(): matrix is singular" as such we utilise bw = 40 (optimal bandwidth obtained for train data set instead): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gwr_pred <- gwr.predict(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK+ PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, data = train_data_sp, predictdata = test_data_sp, bw = 40, kernel = "gaussian", adaptive = TRUE, longlat = FALSE) ``` ::: ::: callout-note ## In-class note from Prof Kam - Likely issue is several points with same postal code hence same coordinates - spatial ML can tolerate but gwr unable to handle hence error of "No regression point is fixed" - Could have averaged HDB resale price but not good idea as different units at the same postal code could have varying prices - Instead, we do a jitter to carry out slight displacement of the points: - note that this [SAS reference](https://blogs.sas.com/content/iml/2011/07/06/to-jitter-or-not-to-jitter-that-is-the-question.html) shared that it's not a good idea as its for aspatial data - BUT jittering in our exercise just change the x, y value of the coordinates and not the attribute values - When it comes to test data, question of whether we use bw used to calibrate train data or whether we determine new bw for test data: - if the former, is bw = 40 for the school of thought to have parity - if the latter, bw = 25, as test data is different from training data Prof shared that [either method above works]{.underline} but what extent to which results will be sensitive to the bw - for HDB property transaction, Prof didn't find much difference. If data set is small, high chance will have variation but if data set is big and use method such as random forest (for which have a lot of randomisation), should be able to resolve. ::: ## 8.8 Preparing coordinates data (for Predictive Modelling via SpatialML method) ### 8.8.1 Extracting coordinates data The code chunk below extract the x,y coordinates of the full, training and test data sets: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coords <- st_coordinates(mdata) coords_train <- st_coordinates(train_data) coords_test <- st_coordinates(test_data) ``` ::: Before we continue, we write the output as new rds files and load into the R environment for future use: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_rds(coords_train,"data/rds/coords_train.rds") write_rds(coords_test,"data/rds/coords_test.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coords_train <- read_rds("data/rds/coords_train.rds") coords_test <- read_rds("data/rds/coords_test.rds") ``` ::: ### 8.8.2 Dropping geometry field In this step, we will drop the geometry column of the sf data.frame by using st_drop_geometry() of the sf package: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train_data <- train_data %>% st_drop_geometry() ``` ::: ::: callout-note ## In-class note from Prof Kam - **note that need to extract coordinates (coords) as dataframe** which will be used to calibrate model - SpatialML unable to use train and test data directly - **note from grf documentation that only can accept dframe** - one for dependent variable and one for independent variable. coords must also be in the sequence x and y. - **need to drop geometry column from train_data to make it from sf data frame to normal data frame**, otherwise will keep getting error when running SpatialML ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} train_data_nogeom <- train_data %>% st_drop_geometry() ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1234) rf <- ranger(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK+ PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, data = train_data_nogeom) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1234) gwRF_adaptive <- grf(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK+ PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, dframe = train_data_nogeom, bw = 55, kernel = "adaptive", coords = coords_train) ``` ::: - note that dframe and coords have to be consistent i.e. both derive from training data ::: ## 8.9 Calibrating Random Forest Model In this section, we will calibrate a model to predict HDB resale prices by using the random forest function of the [**ranger**](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ranger/index.html) package: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1234) rf <- ranger(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK+ PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, data = train_data) rf ``` ::: We save this model as a new rds file and load it into the R environment to avoid re-running the step above: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_rds(rf,"data/rds/rf.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rf <- read_rds("data/rds/rf.rds") rf ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Ranger result Call: ranger(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK + PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, data = train_data) Type: Regression Number of trees: 500 Sample size: 10335 Number of independent variables: 14 Mtry: 3 Target node size: 5 Variable importance mode: none Splitrule: variance OOB prediction error (MSE): 728602496 R squared (OOB): 0.9495728 ``` ::: ::: ## 8.10 Calibrating Geographical Random Forest Model In this section, we will calibrate a model to predict HDB resale prices by using `grf()` of [**SpatialML**](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ranger/index.html) package. ### 8.10.1 Calibrating using training data The code chunk below calibrates a geographic random forest model by using `grf()` of **SpatialML** package: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(1234) gwRF_adaptive <- grf(resale_price ~ floor_area_sqm + storey_order + remaining_lease_mths + PROX_CBD + PROX_ELDERLYCARE + PROX_HAWKER + PROX_MRT + PROX_PARK+ PROX_MALL + PROX_SUPERMARKET + WITHIN_350M_KINDERGARTEN + WITHIN_350M_CHILDCARE + WITHIN_350M_BUS + WITHIN_1KM_PRISCH, dframe = train_data, bw = 55, kernel = "adaptive", coords = coords_train) ``` ::: We save the model output as a new rds file to avoid re-running the step above, since the process takes some time to run, and load it into the R environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_rds(gwRF_adaptive,"data/rds/gwRF_adaptive.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gwRF_adaptive <- read_rds("data/rds/gwRF_adaptive.rds") ``` ::: ::: callout-note ## In-class notes from Prof Kam: - **Query on why bw = 55 is used \>\> Prof shared that same as above steps, will have to calculate bw and use that bw** - note in gwRF_adaptive, LGofFit means Local Goodness of Fit - note that by default trees = 500 for grf function, can adjust ntree to change no. of trees ::: ### 8.10.2 Predicting by using test data #### 8.10.2.1 Preparing the test data The code chunk below will be used to combine the test data with its corresponding coordinates data: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_data <- cbind(test_data,coords_test) %>% st_drop_geometry() ``` ::: ::: callout-note ## In-class notes from Prof Kam ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_data_nogeom <- cbind(test_data,coords_test) %>% st_drop_geometry() ``` ::: - note that above combine test_data with coords_test as next code chunk requires the data in the same table i.e. x.var.name = "X" and y.var.name = "Y", this is different from what was done for train_data under the SpatialML methods as the code required a separate coords file for the coords argument i.e. coords = coords_train ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gwRF_pred <- predict.grf(gwRF_adaptive, test_data_nogeom, x.var.name = "X", y.var.name = "Y", local.w = 1, global.w = 0) ``` ::: - above gives predicted values from test data - make the output into a dataframe: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_rds(gwRF_pred,"data/rds/GRF_pred.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} GRF_pred <- read_rds("data/rds/GRF_pred.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} GRF_pred_df <- as.data.frame(GRF_pred) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_data_pred <- cbind(test_data,GRF_pred_df) ``` ::: ::: #### 8.10.2.2 Predicting with test data Next, `predict.grf()` of spatialML package will be used to predict the resale value by using the test data and gwRF_adaptive model calibrated earlier: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} gwRF_pred <- predict.grf(gwRF_adaptive, test_data, x.var.name = "X", y.var.name = "Y", local.w = 1, global.w = 0) ``` ::: We will save the output as a new rds file to avoid re-running the step above and load it into the R environment: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_rds(gwRF_pred,"data/rds/GRF_pred.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} GRF_pred <- read_rds("data/rds/GRF_pred.rds") ``` ::: #### 8.10.2.3 Converting the predicting output into a data frame The output of the `predict.grf()` is a vector of predicted values. It is wiser to convert it into a data frame for further visualisation and analysis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} GRF_pred_df <- as.data.frame(GRF_pred) ``` ::: We will append the predicted values to the test data via cbind(): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_data_p <- cbind(test_data,GRF_pred_df) ``` ::: We will save it as a new rds file to avoid re-running the step above: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} write_rds(test_data_p,"data/rds/test_data_p.rds") ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} test_data_p <- read_rds("data/rds/test_data_p.rds") ``` ::: ### 8.10.3 Calculating Root Mean Square Error The root mean square error (RMSE) allows us to measure how far predicted values are from observed values in a regression analysis. In the code chunk below, rmse() of Metrics package is used to compute the RMSE. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rmse(test_data_p$resale_price, test_data_p$GRF_pred) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 27302.9 ``` ::: ::: ### 8.10.4 Visualising the predicted values Alternatively, we can use a scatterplot to visualise the actual resale price and the predicted resale price using the code chunk below: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(test_data_p, aes(x=GRF_pred, y=resale_price))+ geom_point() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Hands-on_Ex08_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-60-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: A better predictive model is one that has scatter points close to the diagonal line. The scatterplot can also be used to detect if there are any outliers in the model. ::: callout-note ## In-class notes from Prof Kam - note that as we are doing geospatial, we are interested in the distribution of the results over space - to check if the above means that we will need to visualise the distribution via tmap etc rather than just a scatterplot ::: ::: callout-note ## In-class notes from Prof Kam: - important to first determine bandwidth for gwRF then calibrate model - technically the same bandwidth should be used throughout the geographically weighted models to ensure that samples are consisten - sample size: one predictor should have \~100 observations to have a good predictive analysis. note that random forest will try to overcome if sample size is slightly smaller. in literature, min. 50 rows of data per variable but ideally 100 observations for each predictor :::
